stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 4.7 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 314 K and 0.96 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 27.0 mL of 0.11 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 3 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.13 M NaOH.
3 g of $$\ce{KNO3}$$ dissolves in 86 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 9.8 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Zn electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Zn^{2+}}$$ and a Cu electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Cu^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Zn^{2+} + 2e- -> Zn}$$ E° = -0.76 V; $$\ce{Cu^{2+} + 2e- -> Cu}$$ E° = 0.34 V.
The photoelectron spectra of C (Z = 6) and N (Z = 7) are compared.

questions.stem: How many moles are in 105 g of $$\ce{C3H8}$$?

options.why: Correct. n = m/M with M = 44.09 g/mol.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 26.7 g. The actual yield is 21.6 g. What is the percent yield?
A reaction has a theoretical yield of 35.9 g. The actual yield is 25.8 g. What is the percent yield?
What is the pH of a 0.25 M solution of $$\ce{Ba(OH)2}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
That is the pOH; subtract from 14.
Each formula unit releases two OH⁻.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.25 M; pH = 14 − pOH.

questions.stem: 153 g of water at 78 °C is mixed with 135 g of water at 30 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.
Pair each mass with its own temperature.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 38 kJ/mol, the transition state at 135 kJ/mol and the products at 126 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the forward reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 97, ΔH = 88, reverse Ea = 9 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: Which formula is most likely for the compound of element X (Group 2) and element Y (Group 16)?
Why is the enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?

options.text: Vaporization separates molecules completely, overcoming all intermolecular forces

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{CH4}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
CH4 has a larger molar mass (16 g/mol).
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: He 4, Cl2 70.9, CH4 16, Ar 40.

questions.stem: What is the pressure of 2.37 mol of gas in a 11 L container at 270 K?

options.why: With L and atm, use R = 0.08206.

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 15 L flask at 2.46 atm and 253 K?
A weak acid HA has pKa = 5.4. In a solution at pH 6.7, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of O in $$\ce{H2SO4}$$?

options.why: That is the percent of the other elements.
Use masses, not numbers of atoms.
There are 4 atoms of O in the formula.

questions.stem: What volume does 0.4 mol of gas occupy at 0.528 atm and 338 K?

options.why: Use R = 0.08206 with atm and L.
22.4 L/mol applies only at 0 °C and 1 atm.

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of arsenic (As, Z = 33)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 33 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{CO3^{2-}}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: How should acetic acid be written in a net ionic equation?

options.text: It is always omitted as a spectator

options.why: Correct. It is a weak acid and mostly un-ionized.

questions.explanation: It is a weak acid and mostly un-ionized.

questions.stem: Two buffers have the same pH, but buffer X has ten times the concentration of each component. Which is true?

options.text: Buffer X has a greater buffer capacity
options.why: Correct. More acid and base are available to react.

options.text: Buffer X has a lower pH
options.why: The ratio, and pH, are the same.

options.text: Buffer X cannot resist pH changes

questions.explanation: More acid and base are available to react.

questions.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?

options.text: It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy
options.why: Correct. The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.explanation: The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.stem: Is $$\ce{CH2O}$$ polar or nonpolar, and why?

options.why: Containing H does not make a molecule polar.

options.text: Nonpolar, because its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry
options.why: Consider the molecule's shape, not only its bonds.

options.text: Polar, because its bond dipoles do not cancel
Nonpolar, because it has no polar bonds
options.why: Polarity depends on both bond polarity and geometry.

questions.explanation: CH2O is trigonal planar; the dipoles do not cancel.

questions.stem: A mass spectrum of a sample of bromine shows two peaks: mass 79 with relative abundance 59% and mass 81 with 41%. What is the average atomic mass of the sample?

options.why: Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.
The isotopes are not equally abundant.
Pair each mass with its own abundance.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 1.95 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 814 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
A 33.6 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 29.1 mL of 0.052 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.0173 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 524 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (0.96).

questions.stem: Mechanism: (1) NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO (slow); (2) NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂ (fast). Which rate law is consistent with it?

options.why: CO is not in the slow step.
That is the overall equation, not the slow step.
Correct. The slow first step determines the rate.

questions.explanation: The slow first step determines the rate.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.7 mol N₂, 0.8 mol O₂ and 0.9 mol Ar at a total pressure of 1.5 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: When does a battery's cell potential reach zero?

options.text: When the reaction reaches equilibrium (Q = K)
options.why: Correct. No net driving force remains.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 4.7. In a solution at pH 2, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: A solid melts at 1,710 °C, is very hard and does not conduct electricity. It is most likely:

options.why: Molecular solids melt at low temperatures.

options.text: An ionic solid that conducts as a solid
options.why: Ionic solids do not conduct as solids.

questions.stem: 28 mL of 4.8 M solution is diluted to 271 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of Cl in $$\ce{ClO3^-}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: Which substance has the highest boiling point?

options.why: Correct. Water forms extensive hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 31 L flask at 0.833 atm and 379 K?
For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 5.9. A mixture has [A] = 0.8 M, [B] = 0.7 M and [C] = 0.7 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 1.25
It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.875
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.875
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.875, which is less than K.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.5 mol N₂, 0.6 mol O₂ and 0.7 mol Ar at a total pressure of 1.4 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 14. What is K for the reaction multiplied by ½?

options.why: K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.

questions.stem: Steel is harder than pure iron because:

options.text: Carbon replaces iron atoms of the same size
Small carbon atoms in the gaps (interstitial alloy) hinder layers of iron atoms from sliding

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 18. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{MgF2}$$ or $$\ce{KBr}$$?

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{KBr}$$, because its ions have larger charges
$$\ce{MgF2}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: $$\ce{KBr}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

questions.explanation: MgF2 has ion charges 2 and 1; KBr has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: Which change alters the value of K?
What is the pH of a 0.2 M solution of acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 \times 10^{-5})?

options.why: Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].
A weak acid does not ionize completely.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{2N2O5 -> 4NO2 + O2}$$, $$\ce{N2O5}$$ is consumed at 0.68 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NO2}$$ form?

options.why: Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.
Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 4/2.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.094 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 128 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature falls by 8.1 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 4330 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).
Divide by the moles of reactant.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 0.7 M and [I₂] = 1.7 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 0.78 M. What is K?
For the galvanic cell made from these half-cells, what is ΔG°? (F = 96,485 C/mol)

options.why: Correct. ΔG° = −nFE° with n = 2 electrons transferred and E° = 3.17 V.
ΔG° is negative for a positive E°.

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 4.74) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 40.3 mL. What is the pH after 20.2 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.
Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is -6 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = 2.42; K = 11.3. Negative ΔG°: K greater than 1.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.32 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 4.74) and 0.45 mol of its conjugate base A⁻. Then 0.16 mol of NaOH is added. What is the pH?

options.why: Correct. First react: OH⁻ converts HA to A⁻. Then pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
Update moles after the added acid or base reacts.

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = 191 kJ/mol and ΔS° = -54 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 507 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).
Convert ΔS from J to kJ.

questions.stem: A compound (octane) is 84.1% C, 15.9% H by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.
Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to C4H9; the molecular formula is C8H18.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -111 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -122 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and reversing reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 1 M solution of nitrous acid (Ka = 4.5 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 4; doubling [B] multiplies it by 2.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×4, so order 2 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×2, so order 1 in B.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is built from Ni/$$\ce{Ni^{2+}}$$ and Pb/$$\ce{Pb^{2+}}$$ half-cells. Which electrode is the anode?

options.why: Correct. The half-reaction with the lower reduction potential runs as oxidation at the anode.
The higher potential is reduced at the cathode.

options.text: Pb, where reduction occurs at the anode
options.why: Reduction occurs at the cathode, not the anode.

questions.explanation: Ni (E° -0.25 V) is oxidized at the anode; Pb is reduced at the cathode.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3}$$, 38 g of $$\ce{Fe}$$ reacts with 95 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{Fe2O3}$$ can form?

options.why: Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Not all of both reactants reacts.
Correct. Fe is the limiting reactant.

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$$.

options.why: Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O(l)}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).
Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{CaF2}$$ is 3.9 \times 10^{-11}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 1.021 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in 1/[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: 2X → X₂. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Zn²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.05 M F⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Explain how lowering the pH affects the solubility.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: Solubility increases: H⁺ reacts with F⁻ (a base), shifting the equilibrium toward dissolving.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of N.
Explain why the 1s peak of N has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of C.

rubric.criterion: N has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: N has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: C: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
